# Conclusions

In this study, we identified three metabolically distinct subgroups among individuals at high risk of type 2 diabetes, characterized by differences in glucose regulation, incretin secretion and glucagon suppression. The subgroups differed markedly in body fat distribution, with the insulin-resistant, dysglycemic subgroup exhibiting the highest visceral and subcutaneous adiposity, while the two more insulin-sensitive subgroups primarily differed in SAT, VAT/SAT ratio and body fat percentage despite similar glycemic status.

Previous phenotyping studies have shown that metabolic heterogeneity is already present before diabetes onset. Wagner et al. [@wagner2021] identified clusters that differed in glycemia, insulin sensitivity and secretion, body fat distribution and genetic risk, and showed that these phenotypes were related to progression to diabetes and their risk of diabetes-related complications. Similarly, Stroebel et al. [@stroebel2025] identified distinct prediabetes phenotypes using clinical risk factors, measures of insulin resistance and beta-cell function, and detailed measures of body fat distribution, showing that body composition further differentiated adiposity-related phenotypes. The present findings broadly align with these studies, as cluster 3 shared features with insulin-resistant phenotypes characterized by higher adiposity, whereas clusters 1 and 2 reflected more insulin-sensitive and normoglycemic phenotypes. Beyond these similarities, cluster 3 showed impaired early but preserved overall glucagon suppression and higher incretin secretion than cluster 1, suggesting a complex response pattern rather than consistent hormonal deficiency. This higher incretin secretion may reflect compensatory or adiposity-related responses, as suggested previously [@færch2008; @vilsbøll2003]. Clusters 1 and 2 differed markedly in their incretin and glucagon responses despite similar glycemic status and insulin sensitivity. Cluster 2 had the highest incretin secretion but lowest glucagon suppression across all clusters, whereas cluster 1 showed the opposite pattern. The low glucagon suppression in cluster 2 may reflect an insulin-sensitive phenotype rather than dysregulation, as suggested previously [@færch2016; @wagner2017]. Notably, cluster 1 had the lowest GLP-1 secretion despite lower glycemia and higher insulin sensitivity than cluster 3, adding nuance to prior evidence linking lower GLP-1 secretion to prediabetes in the ADDITION-PRO cohort [@færch2015]. Together, these findings suggest that OGTT-derived incretin and glucagon responses add another dimension to established glycemic and adiposity-based phenotypes, revealing heterogeneity that standard metabolic classification does not capture.

Beyond hormonal responses, the three clusters differed in their associations with body fat distribution. The insulin-resistant profile of cluster 3 was associated with higher VAT, SAT, VAT/SAT ratio, and body fat percentage than cluster 2, consistent with previous findings from the ADDITION-PRO cohort [@philipsen2015] and evidence linking visceral adiposity to impaired fasting glucose, impaired glucose tolerance and newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes [@borel2015]. Compared with cluster 2, cluster 1 had higher SAT and body fat percentage but a lower VAT/SAT ratio, while VAT was similar. This pattern suggests that cluster 1 may represent a subgroup with relatively more subcutaneous than visceral adiposity despite higher overall adiposity. Higher SAT has previously been suggested to be a protective metabolic trait, as it was found to be inversely associated with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes [@borel2015]. This is also consistent with Stroebel et al. [@stroebel2025], who identified a subcutaneous-adipose group with higher SAT, relatively lower VAT and a more favorable diabetes risk profile than phenotypes characterized by higher visceral adiposity.

Sex composition is important when interpreting differences in fat distribution. Cluster 2 had a higher proportion of women, who would generally be expected to have higher SAT [@bredella2017]. Therefore, the higher SAT and lower VAT/SAT ratio in cluster 1, despite a lower proportion of women, suggest that these differences are unlikely to be explained solely by sex composition. Moreover, sex-stratified clustering produced broadly similar phenotypes in both men and women as in the main analysis, supporting the robustness of the primary clustering solution. Women had higher total GLP-1 and GIP but lower glucagon suppression across all clusters, consistent with previous findings in the ADDITION-PRO cohort [@færch2015]. Although sex-by-cluster interaction models suggested some differences in body fat distribution, estimates were non-significant with wide confidence intervals, indicating statistical uncertainty. Because VAT has been shown to have a stronger association with cardiometabolic risk in women [@schorr2018], the metabolic implications of the identified fat distribution differences may differ between sexes.

The strengths of this study include the relatively large cohort of individuals with NGT, prediabetes and type 2 diabetes, sensitive and specific methods of measuring glucagon, GLP-1 and GIP through the OGTT [@holst1983; @orskov1994; @toft-nielsen2001], and detailed assessment of fat distribution by ultrasound. However, several limitations should be considered. First, the cross-sectional design precludes causal interpretations between cluster characteristics and fat distribution. Second, fully sex-stratified analyses, in which sex-specific clusters were subsequently related to body fat distribution, were not performed, which may have limited the identification of sex-specific phenotypes. Given known sex differences in fat distribution and incretin responses, future studies with larger samples should consider sex-stratified clustering as the primary approach. Moreover, because male sex contributed to the ADDITION-DK risk score [@glümer2004], women in the cohort may have had a higher burden of other risk factors, potentially affecting comparability between sexes. Third, although the study population is referred to as high-risk individuals, some participants had screen-detected type 2 diabetes at the ADDITION-PRO health assessment. Their inclusion should be considered when generalizing to prediabetes populations, but this also allowed assessment of hormonal responses and fat distribution in individuals with untreated diabetes and thereby across all glycemic states. Fourth, as a hard clustering method, K-means assigns all observations to a cluster regardless of how well observations fit in their assigned cluster. The silhouette width of 0.21 indicated limited cluster separation, suggesting that some individuals may not be well-represented by a single cluster assignment [@mori2025]. Finally, excluded participants tended to have higher BMI, visceral fat and HbA1c, suggesting that the included population may represent a metabolically healthier high-risk subgroup, which may have affected both the generalizability of the identified clusters and their associations with fat distribution.

Together, these findings suggest that subgroups defined by distinct postload incretin and glucagon responses also differ in their associations with body fat distribution, supporting the hypothesis that endogenous incretin and glucagon secretion are related to different patterns of adiposity. If incretin and glucagon responses capture metabolic heterogeneity beyond glycemic measures, they may contribute to identifying individuals earlier in their glycemic trajectory. This is relevant because early identification may offer an opportunity for more effective prevention [@tabák2009], and regression from prediabetes to normoglycemia has been associated with lower risk of cardiovascular disease and mortality [@vistisen2019]. Furthermore, frameworks for prediabetes have been proposed that may help inform more targeted prevention strategies [@wagner2026]. Endogenous incretin and glucagon secretion may contribute to such strategies, with the aim of differentiating individuals who require minimal clinical attention from those who may benefit from lifestyle or pharmacological treatment, including incretin-based therapies. In this context, future prospective studies should examine whether endogenous incretin and glucagon responses are associated with different glycemic trajectories or cardiovascular outcomes and different responses to prevention strategies.
